8.text:
In a strictly isotopic sense a steady state 13C-MFA is a stoichiometric
isotopomer balancing problem.

* A stoichiometric model of the network that is to be analysed is
required.  The flux vector v has to satisfy

 S · v = 0

at metabolic steady state and the atom transitions that are implied by
S are the ones which map the input labelling into the intracellular
mass-isotopomer distributions.  Without S the isotopomer balances cannot
be written.

* The data that constrain the flux vector are the measured
intracellular labelling.  In practice the mass-isotopomer distributions,
MIDs, of proteinogenic amino acids or of free intracellular intermediates
obtained by GC-MS / LC-MS / NMR after 13C feeding, together with the
measured extracellular exchange rates, are used to predict the
isotopomer distributions as a function of v and the solution of the
inverse problem is the flux distribution that best reproduces the
measured MIDs.

Enzyme kinetics, the regulatory wiring of the network and the maximal
bioreactor cell density are not used in a stoichiometric isotopomer
model.  13C-MFA is a fluxomic, not a kinetic, method and it is
completely agnostic to regulation.

That is items 1 and 6 in the list.  In practice the stoichiometric
network is closed with a biomass drain reaction.  Writing that reaction
in a chemically explicit way needs the macromolecular composition of the
biomass, i.e. the fraction of protein, lipid, carbohydrate etc. that is
used to convert a measurable growth rate into precursor demands.  The
biomass composition is therefore routinely used in the construction of
the stoichiometric model and is the reason why many implementations quote
stoichiometry + biomass composition + measured MIDs as the three pieces
of experimental / literature information that are normally supplied to a
steady state 13C-MFA.  The core isotopic requirement remains stoichiometry
and measured isotope labelling patterns, items 1 and 6, i.e. two of the
six listed items, three if the biomass reaction is made explicit.

6.text:
In a formal 13C-steady state MFA the flux distribution is obtained by fitting a
stoichiometric / atom transition model to the measured intra-cellular
isotopomer distributions.  In the limit the fitting problem is

* v . S = 0   steady state mass balance
* M(v) = m exp   isotopic steady state

with S the stoichiometric matrix and M the mapping of isotopic label from
substrate to the measured pools.

Hence from the list you need the network that is used in the two equations
above and the experimental isotopic data that is fitted.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry.  Yes. The S matrix and the atom
transition mappings for every reaction in the network are the model that is
used to predict the labelling patterns for a given flux distribution v.
Without the stoichiometry/atom mapping there is no M(v) to fit.
* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates.  Yes.  The
measured 13C fractional enrichments in proteinogenic amino acids, central
metabolites etc. obtained by MS/NMR after feeding a 13C-labelled substrate
in isotopic steady state are the data to which the model is fitted.  The
extracellular rates / growth rate are normally reported together with the
labelling data.

The three items which are normally quoted together with the two above are
the measurable exchange fluxes and the biomass drain that closes the
network.  In practice the biomass drain is written as a pseudo-reaction
whose stoichiometric coefficients are obtained from the measured biomass
composition

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism.  In practice yes.  The
biomass drain reaction that closes the carbon, N, P etc. balances and
converts a measured specific growth rate µ into a specific flux to
biomass, e.g. protein, lipid and carbohydrate precursors, is normally
required to obtain a closed steady state model.  Strictly the isotopic
fitting itself needs only 1 and 6, the biomass stoichiometry being part
of the stoichiometric description of the network.  This is the item that
is most often quoted in textbooks together with 1 and 6, i.e. three
items from the six listed, 1 & 3 & 6, are used to set up a closed 13C-MFA
model.

The remaining items are not needed for a steady state 13C-MFA.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor.  No.  Flux
analysis is per biomass / per cell and is carried out at isotopic steady
state, normally at a given specific growth rate. The carrying capacity of
the bioreactor is irrelevant.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics.  No.  Steady state MFA is stoichiometric / isotopic,
not kinetic.  Kinetic parameters are required for dynamic or kinetic flux
analysis, not for 13C-MFA at isotopic steady state.
* 5. Regulatory networks.  No.  Regulation is not used in the
stoichiometric/isotope fitting problem.

In the minimal textbook formulation therefore the two indispensable items
from the list are 1 and 6, stoichiometry and measured 13C labelling
patterns.  If the biomass drain is counted as an explicit input, as is
customary, the three practical inputs normally quoted are 1, 3 and 6.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: In principle a steady-state 13C-MFA is an isotopomer balance problem.

The isotopomer balances are written for the reaction network

v * S = 0            steady state mass balance
M = f(v,S, T)        steady state labelling balance

so that the formal mathematical inputs to the problem are

* a stoichiometric description of the network that is being analysed, 
  i.e. the set of reactions and the carbon atom transitions that link
  the intracellular metabolite pools together. That is item 1, and without
  it no flux vector can be defined.
* an experimental measurement of the labelling state of the system that
  can be compared with the labelling predicted from the flux vector,
  i.e. the mass isotopomer distributions / 13C enrichment patterns of
  proteinogenic amino acids / intracellular intermediates measured under
  isotopic steady state. That is item 6.

Given S and the measured MID data the fluxes v can be estimated, up to a
common scaling factor, from the isotopomer mapping alone. 

Items 2,4 and 5 are not part of a stoichiometric / isotopomer
balance. Maximum bioreactor cell density, enzyme kinetic parameters,
and regulatory topology are not used in the steady state 13C-MFA
formulation. Enzyme kinetics and regulation are dispensable for the flux
solution and the maximum achievable cell density has nothing to do with
the isotopomer balances.

Biomass composition is the item that is normally added in practice.
Absolute fluxes, and in particular the flux that leaves central carbon
metabolism for biomass formation, are obtained from the specific growth
rate together with a defined biomass reaction. The biomass reaction is
written from the macromolecular composition, i.e. protein / lipid /
carbohydrate fractions, of the organism. If absolute, gDW·h−1, fluxes are
wanted the biomass composition is therefore used in practice to close
the carbon balance and to scale the solution, giving the commonly quoted
practical set 1,3 and 6. If the solution is required only up to a
relative scale the strictly mathematical requirements of the 13C-MFA
are items 1 and 6, two of the six items listed.

4.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution v is obtained from the
atom–balance constraints imposed by the network on the measured
intracellular labelling. In its minimal mathematical form the problem is

S . v = 0                     atom trans. constraints
M(v) . x = 0                  labelling constraints

where S is the stoichiometric matrix of the network that is used and M
is the atom-transition matrix that is derived from the S and from the
measured isotopic enrichment x of the intracellular pools.

Hence the two pieces of information that are absolutely indispensable for
the 13C-MFA calculation are

* the network stoichiometry, i.e. the set of reactions and the atom
mapping that connects substrate to product, and from it the stoichiometric
matrix S and the atom transition matrix, item 1; and
* the experimental isotopic labelling pattern of the metabolic
intermediates that is obtained e.g. by GC-MS / NMR from a 13C labelled
feed, item 6.

Once S and M are known the labelling data x determines the fluxes v up
to the usual degree of freedom that is fixed by the measured
extracellular uptake/secretion rates. The problem is purely
stoichiometric/isotopomeric, it is not kinetic and it does not need
any regulatory information.

Items 2, 4 and 5 are not needed for a steady state 13C-MFA. Maximum
bioreactor cell density, enzyme kinetics and regulatory networks are
irrelevant for the isotopomer balance.

Biomass composition is in practice required in order to write the
biomass drain reaction that closes the network, i.e. to make the
stoichiometry complete.  If the biomass reaction is taken as being part
of the stoichiometric model the biomass composition is already contained
in item 1.  Written out explicitly the three pieces that are normally
quoted in the laboratory are the stoichiometric/atom mapping network,
the biomass composition that defines the biomass formation reaction, and
the measured 13C labelling patterns, i.e. items 1, 3 and 6.  The core
mathematical requirement is the stoichiometry and the labelling data,
items 1 and 6.

1.text:
In a 13C steady state MFA the fluxes are obtained as the set v that
simultaneously satisfies the stoichiometric mass balance

S . v = 0

and reproduces the experimentally observed mass isotopomer
distributions of the intracellular intermediates

MIDexp = MID(v,S,Atom mapping)

in the isotopic steady state. That is all that the method uses.

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry and the atom transitions that go
with it is the network model S on which the mass and atom balances are
built. It is indispensable.
* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, i.e. the
measured mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular metabolites
and the measured extracellular uptake/secretion rates, are the data
that constrain v. They are indispensable.

The method is strictly stoichiometric / isotopomeric. It does not need
any kinetic or regulatory information and it does not need a bioreactor
scale parameter.

* 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor is a process
parameter and is irrelevant for the flux solution.
* 4. Enzyme kinetics and
* 5. Regulatory networks are not used in a steady state 13C MFA; the
fluxes are obtained from balances only. Kinetics/regulation are needed
for kinetic MFA or for dynamic MFA, not for steady state 13C MFA.

Biomass composition is not an intrinsic requirement of the 13C
labeling equations. The biomass formation can be introduced as one
further exchange flux vbio with a pre-defined biomass reaction. In
practice that biomass reaction is normally written from an experimentally
determined biomass composition, i.e. fraction of protein, lipid,
carbohydrate etc., so that the carbon, nitrogen, etc. demand for growth
is closed in S. If the biomass reaction is taken as part of the
stoichiometry it is already covered by 1. In the usual practical
implementation the composition is therefore quoted as a third required
input, giving the conventional set {stoichiometry, biomass composition,
measured 13C MID}, i.e. 1,3 and 6. Strictly speaking the only
methodologically essential items from the list are 1 and 6.

5.text:
13C-MFA at isotopic steady state is a stoichiometric / isotopomer problem, not a kinetic or regulatory one.

The core of the calculation is

* a defined atom transition network : the stoichiometry of the reactions together with the atom mapping that is used to propagate the 13C label through the network; and
* a measured experimental constraint : the experimental 13C labelling pattern of the intracellular intermediates, normally obtained by GC-MS / LC-MS / NMR of proteinogenic amino acids or free intracellular metabolites together with the measured extracellular uptake / secretion rates that set the scale of the system.

Hence in the list

1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry – required. The atom-balanced network, including the biomass drain reaction, is the model on which the isotopomer balances are written.
6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates – required. The labelling data are the observables that the flux distribution has to reproduce.

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in a conventional steady-state 13C-MFA. MFA is a flux-balance/isotopomer-balance method, fluxes are determined from stoichiometry + labelling, not from Vmax/Km or regulation.

3. Biomass composition is not an independent experimental input for the isotopomer calculation per se. It is used in practice to formulate the stoichiometric coefficients of the biomass formation reaction that is part of item 1, and to put the fluxes on an absolute scale when extracellular rates are normalised to biomass. If the biomass reaction is taken as already given in the stoichiometric model item 1 is sufficient; if the model has to be built from scratch the composition is needed to define that reaction. This is the usual reason for quoting three items, 1,3 and 6, for a closed 13C-MFA system.

In the strict minimal data sense the 13C-MFA problem is stoichiometry + labelling, i.e. 2 of the 6 listed items, items 1 and 6.

7.text:
In a steady state 13C-MFA the flux distribution is obtained by fitting a
stoichiometric / atom transition network to the measured mass isotopomer
distributions. The core of the problem is an isotopomer balance

dX/dt = 0 = f(S, v, T)

where S is the stoichiometric matrix, T is the atom transition mapping and
v is the unknown flux vector. X is the set of mass isotopomer
distributions of the intracellular metabolites that are measured.

Hence the formal mathematical inputs that are needed are

* a stoichiometric description of the network that is to be analysed,
  including the atom mappings that tell how carbon atoms are
  rearranged in each reaction, i.e. item 1. The stoichiometric matrix is
  the model on which the carbon balance and the isotopomer balances are
  built. Extracellular exchange fluxes and a growth rate are normally
  measured in the experiment and are used to close the network, but they
  are not among the six items listed.

* the experimental isotopic data that constrain the fluxes, i.e. the
  measured isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates,
  normally proteinogenic amino acids or intracellular polar metabolites
  obtained by MS/NMR after feeding of a 13C tracer, i.e. item 6.

That is all that is required in principle for the isotopomer
calculation. 

Maximum cell density in a bioreactor, item 2, is a process / scale-up
parameter and is not used in the isotopomer mass balances. Steady state
13C-MFA is a stoichiometric, not a kinetic, method so enzyme kinetic
parameters, item 4, and the regulatory network, item 5, are not required.
In particular MFA is not a kinetic simulation.

Biomass composition, item 3, is not a strict isotopomer input. The
biomass reaction can be written once the overall stoichiometry of
central metabolism is defined and the biomass formation flux is fixed by
the measured growth rate / extracellular fluxes. In practice the
biomass reaction is normally written from a measured biomass
composition, protein/lipid/carbohydrate fraction, so the biomass
composition is used in the conventional workflow to define the sink
reaction that closes the network. In that operational sense items 1,3
and 6 are used, i.e. two strictly formal items, 1 and 6, and in
practice three items 1,3 and 6. The items 2,4 and 5 are not needed for
a steady state 13C-MFA.

3.text:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
mass and atom balances of the network together with the experimental
isotopomer data.  The mathematical problem that is solved is

* Sv = 0    metabolic steady state
* f(v, X0) = Xmeas

S is the network stoichiometry with explicit carbon atom mappings and
f(v,X0) is the isotopomer mapping from the unknown intracellular fluxes
v and the known input labeling X0 to the labeling that is predicted for
the intracellular pools. 

Hence the two indispensable pieces of information are

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, with atom transition mapping.
  The stoichiometric matrix S and the atom mapping define the
  isotopomer balances that link fluxes to labeling. Without a defined
  network with correct carbon transitions no flux solution can be
  constructed.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, normally
  obtained as the mass isotopomer distribution of proteinogenic amino
  acids / intracellular metabolites by MS/NMR and of the 13C labelled
  substrate. Those measurements are the experimental data that the
  flux solution has to reproduce.

That is the core of 13C-MFA. 

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme
kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in the steady state
isotopomer balance. Kinetic parameters and regulation are not required
for a flux estimate at metabolic steady state, and the absolute cell
density is a scale up / bioprocess parameter, not a flux-identifiability
parameter. Extracellular rates are normally normalised per biomass and
therefore the absolute density is irrelevant.

In practice the network is closed with a biomass drain reaction. The
biomass reaction stoichiometry is built from the biomass composition

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. fraction of protein,
lipids and carbohydrates

and is therefore normally supplied together with 1.  If the biomass
reaction is counted as an explicit input apart from the central carbon
stoichiometry the practical implementation uses 1, 3 and 6, three of the
six items listed, the two strictly mathematical requirements remaining
1 and 6. This is the usual “stoichiometry + labeling” statement of
13C-MFA.

public_text.3:
In a classical steady state 13C-MFA the fluxes are obtained from the
mass and atom balances of the network together with the experimental
isotopomer data.  The mathematical problem that is solved is

* Sv = 0    metabolic steady state
* f(v, X0) = Xmeas

S is the network stoichiometry with explicit carbon atom mappings and
f(v,X0) is the isotopomer mapping from the unknown intracellular fluxes
v and the known input labeling X0 to the labeling that is predicted for
the intracellular pools. 

Hence the two indispensable pieces of information are

* 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry, with atom transition mapping.
  The stoichiometric matrix S and the atom mapping define the
  isotopomer balances that link fluxes to labeling. Without a defined
  network with correct carbon transitions no flux solution can be
  constructed.

* 6. Isotope labeling patterns of metabolic intermediates, normally
  obtained as the mass isotopomer distribution of proteinogenic amino
  acids / intracellular metabolites by MS/NMR and of the 13C labelled
  substrate. Those measurements are the experimental data that the
  flux solution has to reproduce.

That is the core of 13C-MFA. 

2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme
kinetics and 5. Regulatory networks are not used in the steady state
isotopomer balance. Kinetic parameters and regulation are not required
for a flux estimate at metabolic steady state, and the absolute cell
density is a scale up / bioprocess parameter, not a flux-identifiability
parameter. Extracellular rates are normally normalised per biomass and
therefore the absolute density is irrelevant.

In practice the network is closed with a biomass drain reaction. The
biomass reaction stoichiometry is built from the biomass composition

* 3. Biomass composition of the organism i.e. fraction of protein,
lipids and carbohydrates

and is therefore normally supplied together with 1.  If the biomass
reaction is counted as an explicit input apart from the central carbon
stoichiometry the practical implementation uses 1, 3 and 6, three of the
six items listed, the two strictly mathematical requirements remaining
1 and 6. This is the usual “stoichiometry + labeling” statement of
13C-MFA.

* 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates. The measured

8.text:

S · v = 0
Xmeas = f(v,S,T)

S·v = 0            metabolic steady state

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains fully stable and convergent across rounds 0-4 on the formal mathematical core of steady-state 13C-MFA.

Core agreement across rounds 0-4:
* Flux solution is Sv = 0 and isotopic steady state M(v,S,T)=Mexp.
* Item 1. Metabolic reaction stoichiometry with carbon atom transition mapping is indispensable – defines S and atom transition matrix T that allows M(v) to be constructed.
* Item 6. Isotope labelling patterns of metabolic intermediates, i.e. measured mass isotopomer distributions of intracellular pools / proteinogenic amino acids and 13C input labelling, are the experimental data that constrain v. Indispensable.
* Items 2. Maximum cell density of the organism in a bioreactor, 4. Enzyme kinetics, 5. Regulatory networks are not used. MFA is stoichiometric/isotopomeric, not kinetic/regulatory, and bioreactor carrying capacity is a process scale-up parameter, not an identifiability parameter.

Biomass composition nuance persists unchanged into round 4:
* Strictly formal isotopomer fitting needs only 1 and 6. Biomass formation can be treated as a drain reaction v_bio already contained in S.
* Practically the biomass drain reaction is written from measured macromolecular composition – fraction protein, lipid, carbohydrate – to close the network and put fluxes on an absolute per biomass/gDW h⁻¹ scale. Colleagues therefore routinely quote the practical set {1,3,6} as the three inputs normally supplied, with 1+6 being the methodological minimum.
* All eight colleagues in round 4 state the same two statements: minimal mathematical requirement = items 1 and 6, two of the six items; operationally closed model = items 1,3,6, three of the six items. Items 2,4,5 are never required.

Current understanding: Minimal methodological requirement = 2 items, 1 and 6. Operationally closed textbook implementation = 3 items, 1,3,6. Items 2,4,5 are not required. Unresolved for final answer remains whether the question wants the strict mathematical count =2 or the conventional practical count =3. No new evidence in round 4 changes prior assessment; disagreement is consistent and stable, with unanimous reporting of both the formal minimum and the conventional practical set.
